extracted.intended_audience: practitioners before the USPTO; attorneys subject to USPTO professional conduct rules and disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Assessment of alleged professional misconduct by a practitioner before the USPTO and federal courts, focusing on unauthorized practice of law, misrepresentations to tribunals, violation of local pro hac vice rules, and related USPTO regulatory provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a) — disreputable or gross misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: "[a] practitioner shall not engage in disreputable or gross misconduct;"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to evaluate conduct such as 'playing fast and loose' with court rules, actions that 'violated the ordinary standard of professional obligation and honor,' or that 'hampered the efficient and proper operation of the courts or of ancillary systems upon which the courts rely.' The decision applies this standard where the record establishes misconduct by clear and convincing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5) — conduct prejudicial to administration of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: "[a] practitioner shall not engage in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice;"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to behavior that undermines court processes (e.g., drafting filings for pro se litigants while not admitted, failing to follow court orders, or otherwise causing dismissal or inefficiency). The tribunal treats repeated warnings and continued noncompliance as evidence supporting this violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.505 — unauthorized practice of law / assisting another to do so
rubrics_metrics.description: "[a] practitioner shall not practice law in a jurisdiction in violation of the regulation of the legal profession in that jurisdiction, or assist another in doing so."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violation established by evidence that a practitioner provided legal services (drafting complaints, legalizing lay descriptions, preparing substantive motions/oppositions) while not admitted in the jurisdiction or not admitted pro hac vice. Not signing documents to ‘avoid appearing’ does not avoid the rule. The tribunal treats notations like 'THIS AND ALL RELATED DOCUMENTS WERE PREPARED WITH THE AID OF [NAME]' and witness testimony that the practitioner drafted or substantially edited documents as indicia of practicing law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local Rule LR 83.1(d) — pro hac vice admission and associate counsel requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Local rule provisions: only members of the district bar may appear; a non-member may be admitted pro hac vice by written motion; motion must indicate good standing in another jurisdiction, agree to submit to local rules of conduct, and in civil cases explain compliance with associate counsel requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific procedural requirements: pro hac vice fee ($75), contemporaneous ECF registration forms and any other ECF documentation, and possible revocation of admission if registration documents not filed within 14 days. Associate counsel requirement: nonqualified lawyers must associate with qualified counsel who enters written appearance and signs filings; nonqualified lawyers must not tender filings unless associate counsel has entered appearance and signed. Failure to comply supports finding of unauthorized practice or other sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'practice of law' (Iowa Supreme Court formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The practice of law includes the obvious: representing another before the court. But the practice of law includes out-of-court services as well. For example, one who gives legal advice about a person's rights and obligations under the law is practicing law. Or one who prepares legal instruments affecting the rights of others is practicing law. Or one who approves the use of legal instruments affecting the rights of others is practicing law."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to determine whether drafting pleadings, giving legal advice to pro se litigants, or preparing legal instruments constitutes unauthorized practice even if the practitioner did not formally sign filings or appear in court.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(1) — false statements of fact or law to a tribunal
rubrics_metrics.description: "[a] practitioner shall not knowingly make a false statement of fact or law to a tribunal or fail to correct a false statement of material fact or law previously made to the tribunal by the practitioner."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corresponds to ABA Model Rule 3.3 and frames a practitioner's duty as an officer of the court to avoid conduct that undermines adjudicative integrity. The rule recognizes that, in some circumstances, a practitioner's failure to disclose is the equivalent of an affirmative misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c) — dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corresponds to ABA Model Rule 8.4 and covers a variety of dishonest acts. In some jurisdictions (as discussed with Iowa precedent), misrepresentation requires proof of intent to deceive; courts examine whether the effect of the conduct is to mislead rather than to inform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof — clear and convincing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations of the cited professional conduct rules are found where the record establishes misconduct 'by clear and convincing evidence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tribunal repeatedly applies the 'clear and convincing' evidentiary standard to determine whether the practitioner's conduct violated USPTO rules and to distinguish negligent or inadvertent conduct from intentional misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional/intent element for misrepresentation (Iowa law)
rubrics_metrics.description: "[M]isrepresentation requires proof of intent to deceive." (Iowa Supreme Court precedents cited: Kersenbrock, Smith)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Iowa authority, to prove a violation for misrepresentation or deceit the OED (or accuser) must show intent to deceive; absent clear and convincing evidence of intent, negligent omission or imprecise wording may not meet the threshold for §11.303(a)(1) or §11.804(c) violations. The tribunal contrasts this intent requirement with the conduct-based prohibition of unauthorized practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicia and examples of unauthorized practice or prejudicial conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts the tribunal treats as evidence of unauthorized practice or prejudicial conduct include drafting complaints and oppositions for pro se plaintiffs, providing legal advice and 'legaliz[ing]' client descriptions, using notations like 'prepared with the aid of [attorney],' drafting substantive filings while not admitted or while suspended, and continuing such conduct after court warnings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tribunal considers documentary notations, witness testimony about the practitioner's drafting and advisory role, failure to obtain pro hac vice admission, failure to disclose suspension, and continued similar behavior after prior warnings as persuasive evidence. Conversely, absence of evidence that the practitioner knew his suspension removed 'admitted' status may mitigate findings on misrepresentation claims.
